title: Purifying, growing
hook: the word means both to purify and to grow

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer as rest, and your line: rest in it. Did a stop in your day feel like rest instead of a delay? Today, the prayer is behind us, and a new pillar begins. Day one thousand ninety-three.

A gardener walks out with shears and starts cutting a healthy rosebush. Whole stems, buds still on them, onto the ground. Someone watching winces: you're ruining it. And the gardener says, wait until spring. A cut in the right place, and the plant comes back fuller than before. Taking away is how it grows. Hold onto that picture, because one of the pillars of Islam is built on a word that does the same strange thing. Its name is usually translated as alms, or charity, or the poor-due. But the word itself carries two meanings at once, and they sound like they point in opposite directions. Today, zakat.
screen: `A GARDENER CUTS A HEALTHY ROSE.` → `TAKING AWAY, AND IT GROWS.` → `A PILLAR: ZAKAT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Zakat comes from a root, z-k-w, that the classical Arabic dictionaries give two senses for: to be pure, and to grow, to increase. Lane's Arabic-English lexicon lists both. So zakat is, in one word, a cleaning and a growing. Second, the Qur'an uses both senses together. In surah nine the Prophet ﷺ is told, in Pickthall's words: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Notice who is purified. Not the money. Them. The givers. The verse speaks of the alms doing something to the person who gives, not only to the person who receives. Third, the growing. The Qur'an pictures spending in Allah's way as a single grain that sprouts seven ears, with a hundred grains in every ear. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet ﷺ say that charity does not decrease wealth. On a calculator, that can't be right: you give some away, you have less. The tradition is pointing at a different kind of arithmetic, where what grows is blessing, and the giver. Fourth, why it's a pillar and not just a kind thing to do. Zakat isn't a mood of generosity. It's an obligation, measured and regular, with rules about who pays, how much, and to whom, and the next days on this path will walk through them one at a time. But underneath all the rules sits this word. The rules give the amount. The word gives what it's for: in the verse, the giver made clean, and something in the world made bigger. That turns the question around. Not how much is lost, but what is this making room for.
screen: `ONE ROOT: TO BE PURE, TO GROW.` · `PURIFY THEM, MAKE THEM GROW.` · `A GRAIN, SEVEN EARS.` · `A PILLAR, NOT A MOOD.` · then, large: `WHEREWITH THOU MAYST PURIFY THEM AND MAYST MAKE THEM GROW.`

segments.voice: The practice: give something, and notice the lightness. It doesn't have to be money or large. Before the bell, choose one thing to give today: a few coins, a meal, an hour, a coat you don't wear. Now sit with the choice. Breathe in, and notice whatever part of you wants to hold on. Breathe out, and picture it already given. Notice what happens in your chest, your shoulders. Heavier, lighter, no change. Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Zakat. A pillar of Islam: a set share of wealth given each year. From a root that means both to purify and to grow. Today's word.
Your line: giving makes it grow. Today, give the thing you chose, and afterward, check whether anything in you feels cleaner. Tomorrow: who pays. Day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Muslims who meet the conditions pay zakat as a set share of their wealth each year, and teachers describe it with Qur'an 9:103 as purifying the giver as well as helping the receiver.
